title: ENVO Announces Their First Full Suspension eMTB – The Affordable M50
content:
ENVO is based in Vancouver, B.C., home to the world-famous North Shore trails where trail riding evolved into freeride with ladder bridges, big drops, and lots of gnarly terrain. Until now, ENVO has mostly produced commuter ebikes, but since many of their staff ride trails, a full-suspension eMTB has now joined ENVO’s lineup.

The M50 is an accessibly priced eMTB. It features the company’s own motor and battery, X-Fusion and DNM suspension, MX wheels, and a wide-range 9-speed drivetrain. The frame is available in two sizes. These specs won’t blow away anyone familiar with top-of-the-line eMTBs, but the M50’s price presents a reasonable option for those who are curious about stepping into assisted trail riding.

ENVO M50 – Key Specs:

The M50 is an all-mountain eMTB, featuring a hydroformed 6061-T6 aluminum frame. The frame offers 150mms of rear travel, and the bike comes with a 160mm X-Fusion fork. ENVO went with an MX wheelset for the M50, with no mention of full 29er compatibility.

It’s clear ENVO did their research on suspension linkages, as their first full-suspension eMTB is presented with leverage ratio, axle path, anti-squat, and anti-rise charts. That data reveals the M50’s four-bar linkage aims to deliver the same performance aspects as any of today’s high-end eMTBs.

ENVO says their linkage is designed for initial sensitivity, but gets progressive enough to resist hard impacts and bottom-outs. It also provides a slightly rearward axle path, which typically translates to very good absorption of sharper hits. Anti-squat was tuned to ensure maximized pedal efficiency when you’re in your lowest gears, but deeper in the travel it drops off to offer responsive suspension action. The M50’s anti-rise aims to keep your rear wheel planted under light or strong braking forces.  

The air-sprung rear shock is one component that reflects the M50’s price tag. It is made by a company I’m not familiar with called DNM. The shock features adjustable rebound and a two-position Open/Firm switch. It is tuned to provide plush sensitivity over small bumps and ample support against bigger impacts. The shock is a 210x55mm unit, so upgrading it is a possibility.

As for gearing, the M50 is equipped with a 9-speed Microshift drivetrain. The 9-speed cassette does offer a wide gear range (11-46t), but comparatively the ‘high-end standard’ 12-speed drivetrain provides lower gearing and finer increments. The M50 frame does use a Boost 148x12mm rear axle, so the bike could be upgraded to 12-speed (or even the supremely durable 11-speed Linkglide Shimano components).

One nice inclusion on the M50’s build is a 170mm travel dropper post. Something this frame lacks is a UDH-compatible dropout, instead using its own replaceable derailleur hanger. The frame also features a water bottle mount on the down tube, and the bike comes with an upper chain guide.

Drive System:

The M50 is assisted by an Ananda M230 Motor. This mid-drive motor uses both torque and cadence sensors to deliver pedal assist power up to 20mph.

The M230 motor provides 350W of power, which is not much compared to most full-powered eMTBs that crank out 750W… let alone many ‘lite’ or ‘SL’ class eMTBs that still offer more. Interestingly, the motor does produce 100Nm max torque, which is far more competitive with today’s high-end eMTBs.  

The motor is powered by ENVO’s 50 Series battery. It is a 48V, 15Ah lithium-ion battery offering 720Wh of capacity. The battery performs well in cold temperatures and has its own Battery Management System (BMS) to prevent overcharging or faults. This helps to ensure consistent performance and longevity. Fully charging the battery should take 6-8 hours. The bike’s max range is listed at a very optimistic 150 km, so it’s hard to say how that would translate to miles or elevation on MTB trails.  

The M50’s handlebar display unit has a color display and connects to the motor via Bluetooth. Since the M50’s electronics use CANBUS communication, the display can show you the status of your battery’s health and provide diagnostic info on top of the usual ride metrics. The battery and charger also communicate to ensure safe charging.

Geometry:

The M50 is available in two frame sizes – S/M and L/XL. ENVO says these options should fit riders from 5’2” to 6’4”. Given that most well-known eMTB brands would have three or four sizes covering that height range, I’d say ENVO is stretching a bit with only two.

Reach on the S/M is 440mm, and the L/XL grows considerably to 485mm. The M50’s 64° head angle is appropriate and up to date, and its 77° seat tube angle should offer a strong pedalling position. Rear ends for both frame sizes are 450mm. It might be nice to see two different rear ends, as 450mm is on the long side for the small frame and on the short side for the large. 

ENVO M50 Build Specs:

The M50 is an entry-level eMTB, so you won’t see many fancy brand names in the build spec. Components like rims, hubs, crank arms, grips, the dropper post and saddle, plus the display unit/controller are all from generic suppliers.

Some key components of the M50’s spec are an X-Fusion Trace 36 160mm fork and a DNM AO-38RC rear shock. The 1×9 drivetrain is comprised of Microshift’s Advent components.

Tektro handles stopping duties with a set of HD-M535 four-piston hydraulic disc brakes, on 203mm rotors front and rear. The rims are wrapped with WTB Trail Boss tires – 29×2.6” front and 27.5×2.4” rear. Up front, the M50 gets a 780mm-wide ZOOM handlebar with a 35mm clamp, and a pair of Wellgo flat pedals are included. For complete build specs, check out ENVO’s website.

MSRP for the ENVO M50 is $3,199 USD. Frame color options are maroon or aquatic.

author: Steve Fisher
